references.text: Lot urged the angels to stay with him, just as the disciples urged Jesus to stay with them. Lot said: "Turn aside to me, my lords" and "he urged them strongly" ([ref:1 Mos 19:2-3|Genesis 19:2-3]). The Greek παρεβιάσαντο (to urge/compel) reflects the same eagerness of hospitality.
"And he urged them strongly, and they turned in to him" ([ref:1 Mos 19:3|Genesis 19:3]). Same pattern: an eager invitation to hospitality leads the guest into the house.

In [ref:Dom 19:9|Judges 19:9] it says "The day is wearing on, and evening draws near", which is very close to the wording in Luke 24:29 about how "the day is nearly over, and evening has already come". In both places, the coming of evening is given as a reason to stay overnight.

Rebekah invites Abraham's servant: "There is plenty of straw and fodder with us, and room to spend the night" ([ref:1 Mos 24:25|Genesis 24:25]). An example of Old Testament hospitality where one urges the traveler to stay.
Lydia "urged us" (παρεβιάσατο) to stay at her house ([ref:Apg 16:15|Acts 16:15]). The same Greek verb is used as in Luke 24:29 about urging someone to accept hospitality.

"Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it" ([ref:Hebr 13:2|Hebrews 13:2]). The disciples on the road to Emmaus welcomed the risen Lord when they showed hospitality – a principle emphasized here.

Jacob said: "I will not let you go unless you bless me" ([ref:1 Mos 32:26|Genesis 32:26]). Just as the disciples held Jesus back, Jacob held back God's angel – in both cases, the insistent request to stay leads to a revelation.
"The sun sets" – The Preacher describes daylight that is fading ([ref:Fork 1:7|Ecclesiastes 1:7]). A thematic parallel to "the day is nearly over" in Luke 24:29.

The immediate context: Jesus "made as though he would have gone further" ([ref:Luk 24:28|Luke 24:28]). The disciples' urging in verse 29 is a direct response to Jesus' action in verse 28, showing that hospitality reveals his identity.
